segments.title: The Fog and the Court: Opening the Labyrinth

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried conversation about one of the greatest novels in the English language.

Over the course of this series, we'll be moving through Dickens's vast, fog-drenched masterpiece chapter by chapter — reading it carefully, arguing about it lovingly, and asking why it still grips readers more than a hundred and seventy years after it first appeared.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the fog, the Court of Chancery, and Dickens's extraordinary decision to open this enormous novel not with a character or a scene, but with a condition.
Three brilliant readers have joined me around the table, and I want to introduce them properly — because each of them brings something quite distinct to this book.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and is a novelist in her own right — she reads Dickens as a fellow practitioner, fascinated by how the machinery works, how a single image can carry a chapter's entire emotional weight.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose devotion to Dickens runs deep — though he'll be the first to push back if he feels the novel is being read as pamphlet rather than as art.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times — she brings the reader's instinct, the love of the line, the sense of what makes you stop and read a sentence twice.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with the opening of the novel.
Dickens doesn't ease us in, does he?
He absolutely does not — and that's the first astonishing structural choice.
Most Victorian novels begin with a person, a place, a family — an anchor.
Dickens begins with weather — or something that masquerades as weather.
The very first word of the novel is 'London' — and then immediately, before we've even drawn breath, the fog arrives.
"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping."
That anaphora — fog, fog, fog — it's incantatory.
Dickens isn't describing fog — he's performing it.
He's making the prose itself slow down and thicken, the way fog does to the air.
And then, once the fog has saturated the world, he delivers the novel's other great subject — the Court of Chancery, sitting at the fog's heart.
That structural move — fog first, court second — is not accidental.
Eleanor is quite right that the architecture is deliberate — though I would want to resist the temptation to read the fog too narrowly.
There is an old critical habit of treating the fog as a simple equation — fog equals Chancery, Chancery equals the system, the system equals oppression.
And that, I think, is rather to flatten what Dickens is doing.
The fog, in this opening chapter, is a profoundly moral atmosphere — not merely a social one.
Dickens writes of the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall, and he gives us this marvellous phrase — the 'groping and floundering' condition of those before the court.
"Fog everywhere" is the human condition of moral confusion — not merely a legislative complaint.
What Dickens understands — and this is where his genius lies — is that institutions corrupt not because they are evil in themselves, but because they become substitutes for conscience.
Chancery is not simply a bad court — it is a court in which hope has curdled into habit.
What I keep thinking about — and what I think gets lost when we leap to themes — is how frightening that opening is to actually read.
When I first read it as a teenager I had no idea what Chancery was, and it almost didn't matter — the prose alone was doing something to me.
There's a sentence in the first chapter that I've never quite got over.

"Never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep, to assort with the groping and floundering condition which this High Court of Chancery, most pestilent of hoary sinners, holds this day in the sight of heaven and earth."
'Most pestilent of hoary sinners' — I mean, that's not analysis, that's denunciation.
Dickens is in a fury here, and he doesn't bother to disguise it.
But what I also love is the rhythm — 'never can there come fog too thick, never can there come mud and mire too deep' — the doubling, the insistence, the way it piles up like the fog itself.
Edmund, you said 'habit' — and I think that's exactly right, because what Dickens is capturing in the rhythm is the habitual quality of the suffering.
That's a very perceptive point, Caroline — and it connects to something I find underappreciated about this opening.
The third-person narrator of these early chapters is not — contrary to what some readers assume — a dispassionate observer.
He is a satirist of the old school — Swiftian, almost — whose contempt is perfectly controlled.
When Dickens describes the Lord Chancellor with his 'foggy glory' around him, surrounded by contending solicitors — there is a savage joke buried in the courtesy of the prose.
The joke is that this court has all the ceremony of justice without a particle of its substance.
And then comes the moment — quite early in that first chapter — where Dickens pivots to the individual human cost.
He names the case — Jarndyce and Jarndyce — and suddenly the fog has a face, or rather, many faces.
Dickens tells us that the suit has become so complicated that no man alive knows what it means — and there's something almost comic in that, and then immediately tragic.
He sets up what I think is the novel's great structural irony — that the case at the heart of everything is utterly hollow.
Whatever the estate of Jarndyce once contained, the court has eaten it.
And every character who enters the novel's orbit is, in one way or another, drawn toward that hollow centre.
The architecture of the whole novel is a vortex — and Dickens plants that in the first chapter, almost invisibly.
And then — just when you've settled into the rhythm of that sardonic narrator — the novel does something that still startles me every single time I re-read it.
The voice changes.
Chapter three and we are suddenly in first person — and the first-person narrator is modest, warm, slightly self-deprecating.
She says — and I always love this opening — 'I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever.'
"I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages, for I know I am not clever."
After fifty pages of savage irony, here is Esther Summerson — diffident, gentle, careful with herself.
The contrast is so violent, and yet it works perfectly.
That dual narration is something we'll be returning to throughout this series — it may be the most daring formal choice in any Victorian novel.
Edmund, before we move on — I want to give you a moment on Esther, because I suspect you read her rather differently from Caroline.
Indeed I do — and I would push back gently on the idea that Esther's modesty is a literary device designed merely to contrast with the narrator.
I think Dickens is entirely serious about Esther's goodness — he believes in it as a moral category.
She is, in the old sense, a virtuous character — and the novel asks whether virtue can survive contact with a system designed to destroy it.
When she says 'I know I am not clever,' she is not being coy — she is announcing a deliberate refusal of the kind of worldly cleverness that Chancery rewards.
Goodness in this novel is not naive — it is, in fact, the most radical stance available.
I don't disagree with that at all — in fact I think you and Caroline are saying the same thing from different angles.
Esther's self-deprecation is both a genuine moral stance and a dazzling piece of narrative engineering.
It allows Dickens to have a narrator who can observe without judging, who can witness suffering without being contaminated by bitterness.
And the contrast with the third-person voice is what makes both voices legible — each defines the other.
Two voices, two worlds, one fog — and we're only at chapter three.
In our next segment, we'll follow those threads deeper — into the first glimpse of Jarndyce himself, and what Dickens does with the idea of benevolence in a fallen world.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Richard's Gamble: The Chancery's Grip Tightens

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been moving through Dickens' great novel with something close to reverence — and today we arrive at one of its most painful trajectories.
Richard Carstone — young, charming, genuinely talented — and the slow, terrible way that Jarndyce and Jarndyce devours him.
With me are Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Eleanor, I want to start with you — because structurally, Richard's decline is doing enormous work in this novel.
It is — and I think it's doing two kinds of work simultaneously, which is characteristic of Dickens at full stretch.
On one level, Richard's story is a psychological portrait of obsession — of how a fixed idea colonises a personality until there's nothing left.
But it's also structural counterpoint to Esther's narrative — her steadiness against his drift.
What Dickens is building — and it's almost architectural — is a double helix.
The more Richard spirals inward toward Chancery, the more Esther reaches outward toward life.
And the prose registers this beautifully — watch how the third-person narrator's language becomes almost feverish when describing Richard's state of mind in the later chapters.
There's a passage where Dickens describes him as one who has been 'blighted in the spring of his hopes' — and that word 'blighted' carries everything.
'Blighted in the spring of his hopes and his prospects — blighted in his youth — blighted in his love.'
That triadic repetition — three blightings — it's like watching a sentence mourn someone who's still alive.
Eleanor is right that the structural symmetry is masterly.
But I want to resist the temptation to make Richard merely a victim of an institution.
Because Dickens is rather more interested in Richard's character than that reading allows.
Mr. Jarndyce tells us very early — with great gentleness, and great precision — that Richard has no staying power.
He drifts from law to medicine to the army, not because Chancery has corrupted him, but because his nature is already disposed to drift.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce is, if you will, the drain that his character was already inclined to flow toward.
Burke would have recognised this — the man who mistakes an inherited expectation for a personal entitlement.
Dickens is quite explicit about it in that marvellous scene where Jarndyce says to Esther something to the effect that Richard looks to the suit for everything — subsistence, standing, even love.
'He has allowed it to become essential to him — he calls it his future.'
That is not the prison of an institution — that is the prison of a will that has surrendered itself.
I hear both of you — and I don't think you're wrong.
But what strikes me as a reader — what has always struck me — is how much we like Richard.
Dickens is very careful about that.
He gives Richard genuine warmth and humour in those early chapters — he's good company, he loves Ada, he has real charm.
So when the suit begins to hollow him out, it hurts precisely because we've been given something to lose.
There's a scene — I think it's around chapter thirty-seven — where Esther visits Richard and finds him thin, distracted, his rooms in disarray.
And she writes: 'He was not the same Richard; he could not look me in the face as he used to do.'
That small detail — not being able to look her in the face — it does more than pages of analysis could.
It tells you everything about shame, and about the gulf that Chancery has opened between who he was and who he is becoming.
Caroline, that detail is extraordinary — and it's Esther's narration that makes it land so hard.
Because Esther doesn't anatomise what she sees — she doesn't say 'he was corrupted by obsession.'
She simply notices. And her noticing is so precise, so tender, that we do the interpreting ourselves.
This is one of Dickens' great formal discoveries in this novel — the first-person narrator who is emotionally intelligent but strategically self-effacing.
Esther never tells us what to feel. She creates the conditions for feeling — and then steps aside.
And with Richard specifically, her restraint becomes almost unbearable to read.
Because you sense that she understands exactly what is happening to him — and can do nothing.
I want to bring in Vholes — because Vholes is essential to understanding what Chancery actually does to Richard.
Vholes is Richard's solicitor — a man Dickens renders with magnificent, controlled disgust.
He is the system made flesh — methodical, patient, bloodless.
Dickens has the third-person narrator describe him — and this is one of the great satirical portraits in English fiction — as follows.
'He is a very respectable man. He has never been suspected of anything.'
That second sentence is devastating.
Not 'he is innocent' — but he has never been suspected.
The distinction is everything. It is a portrait of a system so well-armoured by its own respectability that guilt simply cannot attach to it.
And Richard — who does have a moral sense, who does feel shame — walks into it willingly.
Vholes makes my skin crawl every single time.
And I think it's because Dickens gives him this one gesture — he buttons and unbuttons his black gloves.
Over and over. While he speaks to Richard, while he takes his money, while he delivers what passes for news.
It's one of those Dickensian details that becomes a kind of moral signature — the outward sign of a nature that is perpetually adjusting its surface while concealing its depths.
And Dickens actually gives us a remarkable passage about Vholes — comparing him to other professionals.
'The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself.'
He means it sardonically, of course — but that line is also simply true.
And Vholes is its perfect embodiment — feeding on Richard, feeding on hope, utterly without appetite of his own.
What I find so technically brilliant about the Vholes passages is the predatory imagery Dickens sustains around him.
He describes Vholes as having a cold, wide throat — almost serpentine.
And then there's the extraordinary comparison to a cat at a mousehole — patient, inert, and completely fatal.
But what Dickens understands — and this is the structural genius — is that Vholes alone couldn't destroy Richard.
Richard destroys himself by choosing to believe what Vholes tells him — that the suit might yet turn.
Hope — specifically, irrational hope — is the engine of his destruction.
Which is why I think the novel's real tragedy isn't the system — it's that Richard can't stop hoping.
That is exactly right — and it connects to something Johnson said about the nature of hope.
Johnson observed that hope is itself an indulgence — and that the habit of hoping without working is a form of moral sloth.
Richard hopes magnificently. He simply cannot act.
And the marriage to Ada — which should be a positive step, a commitment to life — becomes instead another thing he has done while waiting for the suit to resolve.
Even love, in Richard's hands, becomes provisional.
Dickens is unsparing here — and I think this is his deepest moral point about Chancery.
It does not merely corrupt the law — it corrupts the capacity for present-tense living.
The scenes between Richard and Ada in the later stages are almost impossible to read.
Because Ada loves him so completely — and she goes to him, she stays with him, despite everything.
And yet Richard can't quite receive that love — he's so encased in the suit that even tenderness from her reads as pity or obligation.
There's a heartbreaking moment when Richard says something like: 'I know you have all made up your minds that I am wrong.'
'But it is my cause — and I must pursue it.'
That 'must' — it's the word of a man who has already lost his freedom while believing he's fighting for it.
Dickens understands that the worst prisons are the ones we insist are sanctuaries.
That image — the prison mistaken for a sanctuary — feels like it radiates outward to touch half the characters in this novel.
And of course, Richard's story reaches its devastating conclusion — a man literally collapsing in the court that was supposed to vindicate him.
Eleanor, Edmund, Caroline — we'll pick up that final act very shortly.
After the break, we turn to the novel's extraordinary ending — and ask what, if anything, Jarndyce and Jarndyce finally delivers.

segments.title: A Woman's Shadow: Lady Dedlock's Dangerous Knowledge

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked — the programme where we take Dickens's great fog-bound masterpiece apart, chapter by chapter, image by image.
Today we are turning our attention to one of the novel's most electrifying figures: Lady Dedlock.
Specifically, the moment her composure cracks — when she sees the handwriting on Tulkinghorn's document and recognises, in an instant, the hand of a man she believed dead.
That moment of dangerous knowledge — what it costs her, what it reveals, and what Dickens does with it technically — is our subject.
Eleanor Hartley is with us, and I know she has been waiting to get at the architecture of that scene since we began planning this episode.
Edmund Leigh is here too — and I suspect he will remind us that Lady Dedlock is, above all, a study in moral consequence.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who I believe has strong feelings about whether this woman is victim or agent — or both.
Eleanor — let's begin with the moment itself, in Chapter Two, when Tulkinghorn produces that copyist's document and Lady Dedlock nearly betrays everything.
That scene is one of the great traps in Victorian fiction — and Dickens springs it with extraordinary precision.
We are in Chapter Two, which is narrated in the third person — Dickens's omniscient voice, that cool, ironic surveyor of the great world.
Lady Dedlock has been established, in the first chapter, as the pinnacle of fashionable boredom — magnificent, untouchable, glacial.
Dickens gives us her famous portrait in Chapter Two — she is sitting in the window at Chesney Wold, and Tulkinghorn is there with legal papers.
And then comes the crack in the ice.
Dickens sets it up with a description of Lady Dedlock's sudden change that is almost cinematic in its abruptness.
He writes: "She has turned a little paler than before, and takes no notice of what is said."
That is all — one plain, declarative sentence, and the ground shifts completely beneath the reader.
What strikes me technically is that Dickens refuses to enter her interiority at this moment.
We see only the surface — the pallor, the arrested attention — and that withholding is the whole point.
Lady Dedlock has spent years performing opacity, and Dickens performs it back at us — we are as much in the dark as Tulkinghorn.
Eleanor is right that the technique is masterly, but I think we should pause on what that pallor actually signifies — morally.
Lady Dedlock is not merely startled — she is, at that precise instant, confronted with the full weight of a life she has concealed.
A child she believes dead — a lover she has never named — and a secret that, if known, would destroy the entire edifice of her position.
Dickens was deeply interested — as was Burke, whom he had almost certainly read — in how a great social position can become a kind of moral prison.
Lady Dedlock's greatness and her guilt are, in a sense, the same thing — both require the same performance of absolute self-control.
And Dickens is quite explicit about this in a passage I find rather magnificent — when he describes her public face as a kind of armour she can never remove.
He observes that she is "perfectly well-bred" — and that the phrase itself is double-edged: bred for this life, broken in for it.
What interests me most, however, is not the scandal but the response — the instant recovery, the way she regains her composure within seconds.
That is not weakness — that is a formidable will.
And a formidable will, however misdirected, commands a certain — one might almost say a tragic — respect.
What Edmund says about the will — yes, absolutely — but I think there's something even more vertiginous happening for the reader in that moment.
Because we, the readers, are given just that fraction more than Tulkinghorn.
We see the change in her face, and even if we don't yet know why, we know it means something enormous.
And that — for me — is the true genius of the scene.
Dickens creates this instant of readerly complicity — we become, momentarily, the people who know Lady Dedlock's secret before we even know what it is.
There's a passage much later — when she goes in disguise to the graveyard where Nemo, Captain Hawdon, is buried — that I keep returning to.
Dickens writes that she stands at the gate of that terrible place and says: "Is he buried here?"
Three words — or four, depending how you count — and they carry the entire history of a ruined love.
She's come in the dark, in a servant's clothes, to stand at the grave of a man the world thinks nothing of.
And for that one moment, the great Lady Dedlock is simply a woman who loved somebody, and lost him, and has been carrying it ever since.
Caroline, that graveyard scene is where the dual narration does something almost unbearable — and I think it's worth pausing on how.
Lady Dedlock's story is told almost entirely in the third-person — Dickens's voice, that omniscient observer.
But Esther, her daughter, tells her own story in the first person — intimate, doubtful, always slightly unsure of herself.
These two narrations are moving toward each other through the novel like tectonic plates — and the graveyard scene is one of the first deep tremors.
What Dickens understands structurally is that the reader is always ahead of Esther — we know the connection before she does.
So when Esther, in her own narrative, describes the veiled woman who passes her in Chapter Eighteen and produces in her some inexplicable emotion —
Esther writes: "I was rendered motionless — not by her touch, but by something in her manner, and the way she looked at me."
Esther doesn't know what she feels, but we do — and that gap between her knowledge and ours is where the tragedy lives.
Dickens has built a machine for producing dramatic irony — and its engine is information that Lady Dedlock must suppress and the reader cannot.
I take Eleanor's point about the structural ingenuity — it is indeed formidable.
But I would resist any reading that casts Lady Dedlock primarily as a victim of circumstance or of a cruel social system.
Dickens is too honest a moralist for that.
Lady Dedlock made choices — she chose concealment over confession, chose the great marriage over the honest life — and those choices have consequences that are moral, not merely social.
There is a moment in Chapter Forty-One — Dickens's great confrontation scene between Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn — that I think crystallises this precisely.
She says to him — and the pride is magnificent even in its desperation — "I have no defence."
That is not the speech of a victim — it is the speech of someone who has assessed their situation with absolute lucidity and found it without remedy.
And there, I think, is Dickens's moral seriousness — not merely pity, but something closer to tragic recognition.
I don't entirely disagree with Edmund — but I think Dickens also makes sure we feel the injustice of how unequally the cost falls.
Captain Hawdon — Nemo — dies in a pauper's room, yes, but he has no reputation left to lose.
Lady Dedlock dies in the snow at the gate of a churchyard, utterly alone, dressed as a servant.
The woman who had everything pays with everything.
And Dickens's description of her end is one of the most restrained, devastating things he ever wrote.
Esther finds her, and writes: "I looked at the face, and saw that it was my mother, cold and dead."
No apostrophe, no lamentation — just the bare fact, and the weight of a word that Esther has only just learned to use.
My mother.
Two words, and they contain an entire novel.
That is — genuinely — one of the most quietly devastating endings in the whole of English fiction.
And I think what we've traced in this conversation is a woman who begins as surface — pure performed composure — and ends as pure fact.
The mask stripped away not by scandal, not by Tulkinghorn's machinations — but by love, and by death.
Eleanor, Edmund, Caroline — thank you for that.
We'll be back after a short break, and when we return we'll be turning to the fog itself — and to Chancery — and to the question of whether Dickens's great legal satire still bites.

segments.title: The Boy on the Crossing: Jo's Witness to the System

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great fog-bound novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together.
Today we're turning to one of the most quietly devastating figures in all of Victorian fiction: Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
He is, in some ways, the most important witness in the whole novel — a child who knows everything and can say almost nothing.
With me to talk through Jo's extraordinary function in Bleak House are three people who know this novel deeply and care about it fiercely.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley brings her eye for craft — for the way Dickens builds his effects from the ground up.
Sir Edmund Leigh is here to remind us that the moral imagination matters more than any political programme.
And Caroline Woodcourt brings the reader's instinct — the felt experience of what Jo does to us when we meet him on the page.
Eleanor — let's start with you. Who is Jo, architecturally speaking, in the structure of this novel?
Jo is one of those characters who seems peripheral and turns out to be absolutely load-bearing.
Dickens places him at the very centre of the novel's connective tissue — Jo links Nemo, Lady Dedlock, Esther, and the whole Chancery world without belonging to any of them.
He is the figure through whom all the novel's social strata are forced into contact with one another.
And Dickens signals this structural importance with an extraordinary piece of narration in chapter sixteen — the chapter called 'Tom-all-Alone's.'
Dickens steps back from the story entirely to address us — the readers — almost accusatorially.
He writes: 'What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the outlaw with the broom?'
That word 'connexion' — it's the novel's great obsession, and Dickens plants it right there with Jo's name attached.
Jo is not just a victim of the system — he is the living proof that the system connects everything, whether it chooses to acknowledge that or not.
I take Eleanor's structural point, and it's well made.
But I think there's a risk in making Jo too purely a symbol — a counter moved about the board to illustrate a thesis about social connexion.
What Dickens achieves, which is considerably harder to accomplish than mere structural ingenuity, is to make Jo a fully felt individual moral presence.
The famous passage in which the coroner's inquest dismisses Jo is not primarily about the failures of institutions.
It is about a boy who knew a man — Nemo — and was kind to him, and is now being told that his kindness counted for nothing before the law.
Dickens writes, with characteristic irony, that Jo 'don't know nothink' — he cannot be sworn, he has no concept of an oath.
'Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don't know that everybody has two names. Never heerd of sich a think.'
The comedy of that dialect — 'sich a think' — is in exquisite tension with the tragedy of what it means.
A child so excluded from ordinary human formation that he cannot even conceive of possessing a surname — that is a moral indictment of a very particular and personal kind.
Edmund, yes — and that passage actually broke my heart the first time I read it, when I was about sixteen.
Because Dickens doesn't let us look away from the specific texture of Jo's ignorance.
He lists what Jo doesn't know — can't read, can't write, doesn't know the Lord's Prayer, doesn't know the Creed, doesn't know the King.
And then Dickens does something devastating — he pivots to what Jo does know.
'Knows that it's hard to keep the mud off the crossing in dirty weather, and harder still to live by doing it.'
That 'harder still' — the gradation of hardship — is Dickens at the very top of his game.
Jo knows the economics of survival and absolutely nothing else.
That gap — between what a child of London knows and what a child of London ought to know — is where the novel lives.
Caroline, you've put your finger on the technique I find most remarkable about Dickens' treatment of Jo.
The negatives accumulate — 'knows nothing, reads nothing, writes nothing' — and then the positive arrives like a blow.
It's a rhetorical structure Dickens uses again at Jo's death — and that scene is where the technique becomes almost unbearable.
In chapter forty-seven, Allan Woodcourt tries to teach Jo the Lord's Prayer at the very end.
'The light is come upon the dark benighted way. Dead!'
That single word 'Dead!' — the exclamation mark after one syllable — is one of the great typographical shocks in English prose.
And then the direct address to the reader: 'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, Right Reverends and Wrong Reverends of every order.'
He turns Jo's death into an indictment of every level of the governing class — and does it in a single syntactic cascade.
That's not sentiment. That's a calculated rhetorical attack wearing the clothes of grief.
I shall not quarrel with Eleanor's admiration for that passage — it is, frankly, magnificent.
But I want to note what precedes it — because Allan Woodcourt's presence at that deathbed matters enormously.

Here is a doctor who has returned from a shipwreck, who has no money, no prospects, no position — and he sits with a dying street child and tries to give him the only gift within reach: the words of a prayer.
Dickens writes that Jo tries to repeat the words 'Our Father' and cannot quite manage them.
'Jo! Did I lose thee? Jo, art thou there?'
The thou — the biblical register — is deliberate.
Woodcourt reaches for sacred language at the moment of death, which is the instinct of a good man — not a reformer, not a polemicist, but a man.
The novel, at its core, believes in the redemptive power of individual human attention. That is not a political argument — it is a spiritual one.
I think Edmund and Eleanor are both right — and Jo holds both truths simultaneously, which is what makes him so hard to read without weeping.
What I keep returning to is the scene where Lady Dedlock comes in disguise to find Nemo's grave — and Jo is her guide.
Here is the highest lady in England, and she needs a filthy crossing-sweeper to show her where the man she loved is buried.
Dickens writes of that graveyard with absolute horror — it is one of his great grotesque set-pieces.
'A hemmed-in churchyard, pestiferous and obscene, whence malignant diseases are communicated to the bodies of our dear brothers and sisters.'
That phrase 'dear brothers and sisters' — the language of the liturgy — lands like a slap in the context of that charnel yard.
And Jo stands in the middle of it, knowing where every plot is, intimately familiar with this place that respectable London has abandoned.
He is the keeper of the novel's most terrible secrets, and he doesn't know it.
That phrase 'doesn't know it' is worth staying with for a moment — because it points to the peculiar narrative position Dickens gives Jo.
Jo is constantly 'moved on' — by the police, by Tulkinghorn, by anyone with even a scrap of authority over him.
And 'move on' becomes a kind of refrain — almost a dark comic motif — until you realise what it actually describes.
Dickens gives the phrase its full ironic weight in a passage that sounds almost like a bitter nursery rhyme.
'Move on. I have not forgotten how the folks in fur and velvet turned me out of sight. Move on.'
The repetition is almost incantatory — it becomes a chant of exclusion, of a life defined entirely by other people's refusal to let you exist.
No other character in the novel is defined so completely by movement — by the negative space of being perpetually displaced.
Eleanor's point about movement is acute — and I think it connects to something that is rarely remarked upon.
Jo is one of the very few characters in this novel who is entirely free of Chancery.
He has no suit, no legacy, no claim — nothing that the court could conceivably want from him or offer to him.
And yet he is destroyed. Not by Jarndyce and Jarndyce — but by poverty, disease, and the simple fact of having been born with no protection.
Dickens understood that the law is only one instrument of oppression — and not always the sharpest one.
Jo does not need Chancery to grind him down. The ordinary operation of a society that will not see him is quite sufficient.
That phrase 'will not see him' feels like the key to everything we've been discussing.
Jo is the novel's great unseeable — present everywhere, acknowledged nowhere.
And perhaps that's what makes Dickens' decision to kill him — slowly, lingeringly, in full sight of the reader — so confrontational.
In our next segment, we'll move to the fog itself — that great opening paragraph — and ask what exactly Dickens is doing when he drowns London in opacity before a single character has appeared.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Nested Tales and Fractured Chronologies: How Dickens Tells His Story

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into something that I think is genuinely one of the most audacious structural decisions in the Victorian novel.
Bleak House tells its story through two entirely distinct narrative voices — and they don't quite add up.
We have an unnamed third-person narrator, speaking in a scorching present tense — and then Esther Summerson, writing her own memoir in retrospect.
With me today are three readers who know this novel inside out.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who finds in Dickens' architecture things the rest of us walk right past.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Bleak House as a profound moral drama — and who will tell us when we're being too clever about it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and responds to it, still, as a reader first.
Eleanor, let's start with you — because I think you've described the dual narration as a kind of formal wager.
That's exactly what it is — a wager that Dickens himself seemed almost to dare himself to make.
Think about what he's attempting: a novel that opens in the third person, present tense, which was itself almost unheard of at that scale in 1852.
And then, within the same chapter division, he switches to Esther — writing years after the fact, full of hesitation and self-deprecation.
The voices couldn't be more different.
The third-person narrator is omniscient, caustic, relentless — it moves like weather.
Esther is intimate, domestic, almost stubbornly limited in what she claims to understand.
And the wager is this: that by putting those two voices side by side, Dickens can give us both the panorama and the human heart simultaneously.
No one had tried that at this scale before.
I'd want to refine that slightly, if I may.
The structural audacity is real — I won't contest that — but I think one must ask what the two voices are actually for, morally speaking.
The omniscient narrator is — let's be honest about it — a polemicist.
It is the voice that attacks Chancery, that satirises Mrs. Jellyby's telescopic philanthropy, that reduces Krook to spontaneous combustion as a kind of grotesque editorial comment.
Esther, by contrast, is the moral centre.
She is what Dickens actually believed in — not systems, but individual goodness practised without fanfare.
She has that beautiful, typically Dickensian quality of not quite knowing how good she is.

There is a passage early on where she describes her little housekeeping keys and says something to the effect that she was always busy and always happy — and it carries an enormous weight of moral argument.
"I had always been told that I was a poor unfortunate child, but I had never known myself to be so before."
That retroactive recasting of her own childhood — that is Dickens' moral imagination at its most delicate.
Edmund's right about Esther's weight, but I want to linger on the experience of that tonal switch — because as a reader it's genuinely disorienting, in the best possible way.
You spend three chapters in that scathing, turbulent present tense — London fog, Chancery mud, everything corrupt and decaying —
and then Chapter Four arrives, and it begins: "I have a great deal of difficulty in beginning to write my portion of these pages."
And just like that, the whole atmosphere changes.
You've come in from a storm and someone's handed you a cup of tea.
But here's what I find so affecting about that line: Esther's difficulty in beginning is not rhetorical modesty.
It signals a whole psychology — someone who genuinely does not feel entitled to occupy narrative space.
And Dickens sustains that psychology across hundreds of pages without it becoming tiresome — which is, when you think about it, a spectacular craft achievement.
That's the thing, isn't it — the unreliability of Esther is of a completely different order to the unreliability we usually talk about in fiction.
She's not withholding information from us strategically, like a Jamesian governess.
She genuinely can't see herself clearly — and Dickens uses that limitation to show us things about her that she would never claim.
Think of the chapter where she nurses Charley through smallpox and then falls ill herself.
She describes the delirium with this strange, fragmented imagery — staircases, a flaming necklace, voices she can't place.
And structurally that illness is the novel's pivot — it's where her chronological narrative fractures most severely.
Time skips; she wakes into a changed world.
The fractured chronology isn't just aesthetic decoration — it's a rendering of how consciousness actually works under trauma.
I think one must be careful not to over-psychologise what is, at root, a narrative convenience — but I take the point about the illness chapters.
What strikes me more forcibly in those chapters is the temporal gap that Dickens deliberately engineers between the two narrations.
The omniscient narrator has already told us — in its cool, present-tense way — that certain things have happened.
So when Esther eventually catches up to those same events, we read her account with a kind of dramatic irony that is almost Sophoclean.
We know more than she knows about her own story.
That is not primarily a psychological technique — it is a classical moral one.
It invites us to love her more precisely because we can see what she cannot.
That gap you're describing, Edmund — it also produces some of the most uncanny moments in the novel.
There's a passage where the omniscient narrator describes Lady Dedlock at Chesney Wold — standing before a portrait that we already sense, without yet being told, is connected to Esther.
Dickens writes something like: "My Lady Dedlock has been bored to death."
"My Lady Dedlock has been bored to death. There is a deadness about her that suggests she is looking for something she will never find."
Now, we won't understand that deadness fully until Esther's narrative fills in what Lady Dedlock has lost — but Dickens plants it there like a splinter in your mind.
And that's a technique that only works because the two chronologies are running at different speeds.
The third-person narrator races ahead; Esther catches up slowly, reluctantly.
And the nested tales within the novel — that's another layer of this altogether.
Because Bleak House doesn't just have two narrative frames — it has stories embedded within stories embedded within stories.
Think of Miss Flite, who carries around her little bag of documents — each one a destroyed life, a case that Chancery has swallowed whole.
She is herself a nested tale — a cautionary story about what the Jarndyce case can do to a person — told entirely in miniature, through a birdcage and a list of names.
And then there's the interpolated tale of Gridley — the Man from Shropshire — who has his own completely separate grievance, his own separate Chancery ruin.
Dickens gives him a full, furious speech in Chapter XV — and it's a complete story in itself.
"I have been dragged for five-and-twenty years over burning iron, and I have lost the use of my right hand in consequence."
That's not a subplot — that's a whole tragedy compressed into a subordinate clause.
Gridley is one of the most undervalued figures in the novel, I think.
What his story does, structurally, is refuse to let Chancery remain abstract.
The omniscient narrator can satirise the institution brilliantly — but Gridley makes you feel it as a human cost.
And notice that he dies, as it were, off the page — reported rather than dramatised.
Which is itself a kind of nested storytelling — the tale within a tale is swallowed by the larger narrative, just as Chancery swallows its victims.
It is a formal choice that carries moral weight.
I want to come back to something Eleanor said about Miss Flite's birds — because her names for them are their own nested tale.
At the end of the novel, when the Jarndyce case finally collapses, Miss Flite releases them.

And she tells Esther their names — Hope, Joy, Youth, Peace, Rest, Life, Dust, Ashes, Waste, Want, Ruin, Despair, Madness, Death, Cunning, Folly, Words, Wigs, Rags, Sheepskin, Plunder, Precedent, Jargon, Gammon, and Spinach.
The list begins in aspiration and ends in farce — that's the entire emotional arc of the Chancery plot told as a taxonomy of caged birds.
When she sets them free, I defy anyone not to feel it.
The birds whose names are the whole story — that image has stayed with me since the first time I read it.
What we've been circling, I think, is this question of how Dickens manages coherence — how he keeps all these nested tales, all these fractured time-lines, from simply falling apart.
In our next segment, we'll look at how the novel's great set-pieces — the fog, the spontaneous combustion, the Dedlock revelation — function as the load-bearing walls in that architecture.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Comedy and Cruelty: The Humor of Bleak House

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've spent time with the fog, with Chancery, with the slow grind of institutional cruelty.
But there is another Bleak House — a furiously funny one.
Dickens is one of the great comic writers in the English language, and this novel contains some of his most devastating comedy.
Today we're asking: what kind of comedy is this, exactly — and what does the laughter cost us?
Eleanor Hartley is with us — she's been waiting, I suspect, to talk about Mrs. Jellyby since we began.
Sir Edmund Leigh is here to remind us that comedy, properly understood, is a moral instrument.
And Caroline Woodcourt is with us — who, I know, has strong views about which characters are funny and which are simply being laughed at.
The thing that strikes me every time I come back to the comedy in Bleak House is how structurally embedded it is.
This isn't comedy as relief — as a rest from the serious business of the novel.
The comic figures are doing thematic work just as hard as any of the tragic ones.
Take Mrs. Jellyby — this magnificent, monstrous figure of telescopic philanthropy.
Dickens gives her that extraordinary physical detail — her eyes having a curious habit of seeming to look a long way off, as if they could see nothing nearer than Africa.
"As if they could see nothing nearer than Africa."
That single clause does everything — it's physically comic, it's satirically precise, and it contains the novel's entire critique of misplaced benevolence.
The comedy is the argument.
I think Eleanor is absolutely right about the structural point, and I'd go further.
The comedy in Bleak House is, at its deepest, a comedy of will — of characters who have chosen a posture toward the world and cannot be dislodged from it.
Mrs. Jellyby is funny precisely because her misdirection is willed, habitual, impervious to evidence.
Caddy's cry — that she wishes Africa was dead — is the most human line in that household.
And Dickens places it there to show us the cost of the mother's self-intoxication.
One thinks of Johnson's remark that the true test of a man's benevolence is how he treats those immediately about him.
Mrs. Jellyby fails that test so completely, so cheerfully, that she becomes a figure of moral farce.
What I want to add — and I feel this every time I read those early Jellyby chapters — is the particular discomfort of the comedy.
We are laughing at the expense of Caddy, of Peepy, of those children tumbling down stairs.
These are real children being genuinely neglected.
And Dickens writes it in a way that makes you laugh and then feel slightly ashamed of laughing.
That's the knife-edge the whole novel walks.
There's a moment when Esther describes the Jellyby household — the bony hand of Mr. Jellyby pressing against the wall in the dark, as if he were trying to push through it.
"As if his troubles, like great trees, had struck their roots into him and he could not be released."
That image is tragic — genuinely tragic — tucked inside a comic scene.
Caroline's point about the knife-edge is exactly right, and I think it leads us to Skimpole.
Because if Mrs. Jellyby is comedy in service of satire, Skimpole is something darker and stranger.
He is the comic villain — and I use the word deliberately — who escapes punishment through charm.
His great speech — about being a child, about having no idea of time or money or anything practical — is a masterpiece of performed innocence.
He declares, with perfect equanimity, something to the effect of: I am a mere child in these matters — I only ask to be free from the painful necessity of thinking about them.
"I only ask to be free from the painful necessity of thinking about them."
The audacity of that — the sheer impudence dressed as sensitivity — is breathtaking.
And we laugh at it, even as we're horrified.
Skimpole is the character who most tests my resistance to politicised reading.
Because one can read him as a satire on laissez-faire individualism — and I understand why people do — but that seems to me to impoverish him.
What Dickens has created is a portrait of radical irresponsibility — a man who has abolished his own conscience and aestheticised the result.
That is a moral failure, not merely a political one.
And the comedy works, as Dickens' best comedy always does, because we recognise the type.
We have all met a Skimpole — someone who has elevated their own parasitism into a philosophy.
Can I bring in Mr. Chadband here? Because he's a different register of comedy entirely.
Where Skimpole is silky and charming, Chadband is oleaginous — a great toad of a man, all spiritual vanity and circular rhetoric.
Dickens gives him this extraordinary oration where he speaks at exhausting length about what is Terewth.
"What is peace? Is it war? No. Is it strife? No. It is lovely, and gentle, and beautiful, and pleasant, and serene, and joyful!"
The comedy there is purely verbal — it's the comedy of magnificent, pompous emptiness.
And yet Chadband is terrifying too — he's using this language to persecute Jo, a homeless child who understands nothing.
The laughter curdles.
The laughter curdles — that's the perfect phrase for what Dickens does.
And I think it's worth noting that the dual narration actually sharpens this effect.
The third-person narrator — satirical, omniscient, relentless — can sustain irony at the highest pitch.
But Esther's voice offers us something different — a generous, unironic witness to the same scenes.
So when the third-person narrator skewers Chadband, we laugh with a kind of savage pleasure.
But when Esther watches the same scene with quiet, baffled compassion, the joke becomes something else.
Dickens has engineered two simultaneous responses — comedy and grief occupying the same moment.
I want to defend one figure who is often discussed as a comic grotesque but who I think deserves rather more credit.
I mean Mr. Jarndyce himself — not his comedy, but his tolerance of it.
Jarndyce sees through Skimpole completely, from the beginning, and yet chooses to extend charity.
There's something in that which Dickens admires — the capacity to hold a comic figure in view without either being deceived or becoming cruel.
The Growlery, the east wind — these are Jarndyce's comic self-concealment, his way of protecting others from his own suffering.
That too is a kind of comedy — comedy as armour worn by a good man.
Edmund's point about Jarndyce moves me — because it brings us to what I find most radical about the comedy in this novel.
The truly dangerous comic figures — Skimpole, Chadband, Mrs. Jellyby, even Turveydrop with his deportment — they are all varieties of self-exemption.
They have each constructed a fiction that releases them from obligation to others.
Turveydrop is particularly perfect — he has made his own figure an object of public art, and lives entirely off his son's labour.
Dickens describes him as carrying himself like a man who has done the world an enormous favour by continuing to exist.
That quality of magnificent, preening self-satisfaction — it is funny, but it is also a study in how selfishness dresses itself in dignity.
The comedy is always, in the end, a moral x-ray.
A moral x-ray — that is a phrase worth sitting with for a moment.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is the absolute consistency of Dickens' method.
The comedy and the cruelty are not separate channels — they run in the same current.
Laughter here is never merely entertainment — it is diagnosis.

In our next segment, we'll be turning to one of the novel's most extraordinary achievements — the character of Esther Summerson herself, and why she remains one of the most contested narrators in Victorian fiction.

segments.title: The Reckoning: Fate, Law, and Moral Design in Bleak House

utterances.text: We've spent this episode pulling at the threads of Bleak House — its fog, its voices, its labyrinthine court.
Now, in this final section, I want to ask the question the novel itself seems to be asking on every page.
Does justice exist in this world — and if not, what replaces it?
Eleanor, you've argued all episode that Dickens is a supreme architect of moral meaning.
Does Bleak House deliver a reckoning — or does it leave us in the fog?
That's exactly the right question to end on, and I think the answer is — deliberately — both.
The court of Chancery never delivers justice — it consumes the suit, the suitors, and finally itself.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce ends not with a verdict but with annihilation — the entire estate eaten up in costs.
But Dickens is too sophisticated a moralist to simply shrug at that.
He builds a counter-system — what I'd call the novel's moral architecture — running beneath the legal one.
It's made of small acts: Esther's housekeeping, Jarndyce's quiet sacrifice, even Jo being kind to Nemo.
These don't redeem the system — but they constitute an alternative verdict on how a life can be lived.
I am largely in agreement with Eleanor here, which perhaps surprises her.
The legal system in Bleak House is not evil in a Marxist sense — it is not a class weapon deliberately forged.
It is something more damning than that: it is a system that has entirely forgotten its own purpose.
Dickens gives us Lord Chancellor sitting in his court surrounded by — as he puts it —
'foggy glory' — presiding over a fog of his own making, which he cannot see through any more than his suitors can.
That image is not political satire — it is moral tragedy.
A man charged with dispensing justice has become incapable of perceiving what justice even is.
That is the reckoning Dickens delivers — not a verdict from outside the system, but the system's own spiritual autopsy.
'Spiritual autopsy' — Edmund, I'm going to be borrowing that phrase.
What strikes me, coming at this from the reader's side, is how Dickens manages the emotional reckoning alongside the institutional one.
Because for most of us reading the novel, what haunts us isn't Chancery — it's specific people.
It's Jo, dying on the crossing, asking whether it's dark or whether it's him.
Dickens writes at that moment — and this is one of his most devastating interventions —
'Dead, your Majesty. Dead, my lords and gentlemen. Dead, right reverends and wrong reverends of every order.'
He goes on — 'And dying thus around us every day' — and it lands like an accusation in open court.
That is Dickens delivering his own verdict — over the heads of every legal institution in the book.
And notice the form of that passage — it's a direct address, a breaking of the fictional frame.
The omniscient narrator steps forward and speaks as Dickens the citizen, Dickens the outraged journalist.
It's the only moment in the novel where the technique itself becomes the argument.
And then — structurally — he returns us to Esther's quiet voice, which is the real counter-argument.
Esther doesn't despair. She doesn't campaign. She acts — specifically, personally, daily.
She is Dickens' answer to the question of what an individual can do when institutions fail.
This is precisely why I resist readings that reduce Esther to a passive figure or a mere domestic saint.
She is the moral intelligence of the novel — more so than Jarndyce, certainly more so than the lawyers.
Consider the scene where she burns the letter from Lady Dedlock — her own mother's confession.
She keeps only what must be kept — the love — and destroys what would destroy others.
There is no legal proceeding that could match the moral weight of that act.
Burke would say — and I think rightly — that the health of a society is measured not in its statutes but in its private virtues.
Dickens, whatever his politics, understood that profoundly.
I want to come back to Richard Carstone for a moment, because I think he's where the moral design is most heartbreaking.
Richard isn't villainous — he's good-natured, charming, genuinely capable in his better moments.
But Chancery gets into him like a disease — Jarndyce says as much, and the metaphor is literal in the novel's logic.
Esther describes watching him change — and she uses this phrase that I find almost unbearable —
'the suit had taken him in its net.'
Four words that contain a whole life's ruin.
And when Richard finally dies — after the case collapses — there's that terrible line where he says he can begin the world.
He means it as hope. The reader receives it as tragedy.
That gap — between Richard's meaning and our understanding — is one of the finest things in Victorian fiction.
It's irony in the deepest sense — not mockery, but tragic double-vision.
And structurally it mirrors the whole novel — where characters believe they are moving toward resolution while we watch them recede from it.
The dual narration keeps enforcing that: Esther's first person and the omniscient third create two different time-horizons.
Esther writes looking back — we know she survived. The third-person narrator writes in an eternal, relentless present.
That architecture tells us: individual lives can be narrated to a good end, but systems grind on regardless.
On Richard — and I say this gently — I think Dickens is also making a classical point about weakness of will.
Aristotle called it akrasia — the condition of knowing the good and failing to pursue it.
Richard is warned — repeatedly, tenderly — by Jarndyce, by Ada, by Esther herself.
He knows the suit is poison. He cannot leave it alone.
The system exploits his weakness, certainly — but the weakness precedes the system's hold.
Dickens never absolves his characters entirely on grounds of circumstance. That is his moral seriousness.
I want to defend Richard slightly — not from responsibility, but from condescension.
He grew up without parents, raised on expectation of an inheritance he could never touch.
The suit isn't just a temptation for Richard — it's the only story he's ever been given about who he is.
Esther had her own darkness to survive — her childhood, her smallpox, her illegitimacy — and she built a new story.
But Esther, as Edmund says, has a moral constitution Richard simply never developed.
The novel holds both truths — his culpability and our sympathy — without resolving the tension.
That unresolved tension feels very true to how the novel ends — with healing and loss in the same breath.
The second Bleak House is rebuilt. Esther is happy — or says she is. Ada has her child.
But Lady Dedlock is dead at the gate of the pauper cemetery, and Chancery has simply consumed itself.
Eleanor — a last word on the ending. Does Dickens earn it?
He earns the sorrow entirely. The happiness — I think he earns most of it.
What's remarkable is Esther's closing — her famous trailing-off, 'even supposing—'

'I know that my dearest little pets are very pretty, and that my darling is very beautiful, and that my guardian has the brightest and most benevolent face that ever was seen, and that they can very well do without much beauty in me — even supposing—'
And it stops there. The sentence doesn't finish. The thought is swallowed.
Dickens has given us a character so conditioned to self-erasure that she cannot complete a sentence about her own beauty.
That dash at the end is not punctuation — it is character, compressed into a mark on the page.
That ending has always moved me — I confess it freely.
But I'd add something about what Dickens does with Jarndyce in the final pages.
He releases Esther from an engagement she accepted out of gratitude — and he does it with absolute grace.
No recrimination, no martyrdom performed for sympathy — simply the act of a good man who wants the beloved's happiness above his own.
Dickens understood — and this is rare in Victorian fiction — that goodness is not spectacular.
It is quiet, consistent, and entirely without audience.
The moral design, then — if I were to name it — is this.
Institutions will fail. Systems will devour themselves. Law will become its own opposite.
But the human capacity for decency — enacted in specific moments, specific gestures, specific words — persists.
Think of Allan Woodcourt, keeping his professional integrity through poverty and war and uncertainty.
Think of Charley, Esther's maid, nursing her through smallpox — a child taking on adult love.
Dickens doesn't offer us a reformed Chancery. He offers us these people.
And in a very quiet way, he asks us: is that enough?
Is that enough — I think that question will stay with listeners long after this episode.
We've ranged today across the fog and the fire, the court and the countryside, the living and the dead.
We've heard from Eleanor that Dickens builds moral architecture in the very structure of his sentences and his narration.
From Edmund, that the novel's deepest question is about individual character — the will to be good — tested to breaking point.
And from Caroline, that the experience of reading Bleak House is itself a kind of reckoning — with justice, with loss, with the extraordinary persistence of human care.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. In the meantime — read it, and read it again.

out, say, five and forty folio on the Wednesday night, you would have

 which—”  Mr. Snagsby

On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain

c48:p128.text:
A very quiet night. When the moon shines very brilliantly, a solitude
and stillness seem to proceed from her that influence even crowded
places full of life. Not only is it a still night on dusty high roads
and on hill-summits, whence a wide expanse of country may be seen in
repose, quieter and quieter as it spreads away into a fringe of trees
against the sky with the grey ghost of a bloom upon them; not only is
it a still night in gardens and in woods, and on the river where the
water-meadows are fresh and green, and the stream sparkles on among
pleasant islands, murmuring weirs, and whispering rushes; not only
does the stillness attend it as it flows where houses cluster thick,
where many bridges are reflected in it, where wharves and shipping
make it black and awful, where it winds from these disfigurements
through marshes whose grim beacons stand like skeletons washed
ashore, where it expands through the bolder region of rising grounds,
rich in cornfield wind-mill and steeple, and where it mingles with
the ever-heaving sea; not only is it a still night on the deep, and
on the shore where the watcher stands to see the ship with her spread
wings cross the path of light that appears to be presented to only
him; but even on this stranger’s wilderness of London there is some
rest. Its steeples and towers and its one great dome grow more
ethereal; its smoky house-tops lose their grossness in the pale
effulgence; the noises that arise from the streets are fewer and are
softened, and the footsteps on the pavements pass more tranquilly
away. In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn’s inhabiting, where the
shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their
sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them
exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a
distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.
c48:p128.summary: The narrator provides an extended, elaborate description of moonlit calm across the natural world, from countryside to ocean, ending with Chancery metaphors for Tulkinghorn's world.
c48:p128.best_quote: In these fields of Mr. Tulkinghorn's inhabiting, where the shepherds play on Chancery pipes that have no stop, and keep their sheep in the fold by hook and by crook until they have shorn them exceeding close, every noise is merged, this moonlight night, into a distant ringing hum, as if the city were a vast glass, vibrating.

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”

cP:p2.text:
But as it is wholesome that the parsimonious public should know what
has been doing, and still is doing, in this connexion, I mention here
that everything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of
Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth. The case of
Gridley is in no essential altered from one of actual occurrence,
made public by a disinterested person who was professionally
acquainted with the whole of the monstrous wrong from beginning to
end. At the present moment (August, 1853) there is a suit before the
court which was commenced nearly twenty years ago, in which from
thirty to forty counsel have been known to appear at one time, in
which costs have been incurred to the amount of seventy thousand
pounds, which is A FRIENDLY SUIT, and which is (I am assured) no
nearer to its termination now than when it was begun. There is
another well-known suit in Chancery, not yet decided, which was
commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than
double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in
costs. If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I
could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious
public.
cP:p2.summary: Dickens asserts the factual basis of his Chancery depictions by citing real cases: a twenty-year suit with seventy thousand pounds in costs and another century-old suit with double that amount.
cP:p2.best_quote: If I wanted other authorities for Jarndyce and Jarndyce, I could rain them on these pages, to the shame of—a parsimonious public.

golden rule, whether I gain by it or lose, and I find that I
generally lose), money is the word. Now, sir, upon the chances of Mr.
C.’s game I express to you no opinion, NO opinion. It might be highly
impolitic in Mr. C., after playing so long and so high, to leave off;
it might be the reverse; I say nothing. No, sir,” said Mr. Vholes,

“The number, sir,” said Mr. Vholes parenthetically, “I believe I have
already mentioned. If Mr. C. is to continue to play for this
considerable stake, sir, he must have funds. Understand me! There are
funds in hand at present. I ask for nothing; there are funds in hand.
But for the onward play, more funds must be provided, unless Mr. C.
is to throw away what he has already ventured, which is wholly and
solely a point for his consideration. This, sir, I take the
opportunity of stating openly to you as the friend of Mr. C. Without
funds I shall always be happy to appear and act for Mr. C. to the
extent of all such costs as are safe to be allowed out of the estate,
not beyond that. I could not go beyond that, sir, without wronging
some one. I must either wrong my three dear girls or my venerable
father, who is entirely dependent on me, in the Vale of Taunton; or
some one. Whereas, sir, my resolution is (call it weakness or folly
if you please) to wrong no one.”

For, on a low bed opposite the fire, a confusion of dirty patchwork,

slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he
ever wished to die, and similar strange questions. That when the man
had no money, he would say in passing, “I am as poor as you to-day,
Jo,” but that when he had any, he had always (as the boy most

c15:p107.text:
“Mr. Jarndyce,” said Gridley with a rough sort of salutation, “you
bear your wrongs more quietly than I can bear mine. More than that, I
tell you—and I tell this gentleman, and these young ladies, if they
are friends of yours—that if I took my wrongs in any other way, I
should be driven mad! It is only by resenting them, and by revenging
them in my mind, and by angrily demanding the justice I never get,
that I am able to keep my wits together. It is only that!” he said,
speaking in a homely, rustic way and with great vehemence. “You may
tell me that I over-excite myself. I answer that it’s in my nature to
do it, under wrong, and I must do it. There’s nothing between doing
it, and sinking into the smiling state of the poor little mad woman
that haunts the court. If I was once to sit down under it, I should
become imbecile.”

“Aye!” said the old man, coming slowly out of his abstraction. “Yes!
Tom Jarndyce—you’ll excuse me, being related; but he was never known
about court by any other name, and was as well known there as—she is
now,” nodding slightly at his lodger. “Tom Jarndyce was often in
here. He got into a restless habit of strolling about when the cause
was on, or expected, talking to the little shopkeepers and telling
’em to keep out of Chancery, whatever they did. ‘For,’ says he, ‘it’s
being ground to bits in a slow mill; it’s being roasted at a slow
fire; it’s being stung to death by single bees; it’s being drowned by
drops; it’s going mad by grains.’ He was as near making away with
himself, just where the young lady stands, as near could be.”
